after: ## Why oil behaves as it does
alt: A cross-section, not to scale. Oil from a tanker floats and spreads as a thin slick driven by wind and currents; lighter parts evaporate in the first days; waves make an emulsion or break it into droplets; heavier residues sink; some washes ashore as tar.
caption: Oil floats, spreads, evaporates, breaks up and sinks or strands: its properties explain the impacts.

alt: A coastal scene, not to scale, with five numbered sources: oil extraction at a sea platform and at a land oilfield that drains into a river; a leaking pipeline on the sea bed; a tanker aground on rocks; a ship pumping oily tank-washing water overboard; and a coastal refinery. Frequent small releases add a great deal of oil over time.
caption: Oil reaches the sea from extraction, pipelines, shipping, tank cleaning and refineries.

alt: A grid of the seven syllabus groups with a physical, a toxic or lethal, and a knock-on effect for each: birds, marine mammals, fish, crustaceans, seaweeds, coral reefs and beaches. For example, oil mats birds’ feathers, is swallowed during preening and stops oiled eggs hatching.
caption: Physical, toxic, knock-on: three effects to give for each of the seven groups.

alt: Two tanker cross-sections, each holed in the outer hull. In the single-hulled tanker oil escapes; in the double-hulled tanker the inner hull, separated by a gap, keeps the oil in. Below, MARPOL is shown as an international convention that restricts discharges, requires oily waste to be kept on board and unloaded at port, and requires records for inspectors.
caption: A double hull reduces the oil released if the outer hull is holed; MARPOL controls what ships discharge.

alt: A grid of five strategies against four recurring limitations. Improved navigation is limited by cost and human error; booms and sorbents by weather and oily waste; detergent sprays by toxicity; skimmers by rough water and slowness; controlled burning by the need for calm conditions and by smoke and carbon dioxide.
caption: Weather, toxicity and waste recur as the limitations of clean-up methods.

after: ## Worked example: matching a strategy to a scenario
alt: A schematic map: a tanker aground in a storm 5 km from a coral reef and a tourist beach, with rough seas for three days. Booms, skimmers and burning are ruled out by the weather; detergent sprays would push oil towards the reef; the plan is booms at the beach and reef entrance when possible, sorbents on the shore and skimming once calm.
caption: Let the weather and location in the question decide which methods you choose.

alt: A bar for a 6,000-tonne spill split into 1,800 tonnes skimmed, 900 tonnes taken up by sorbents and 3,300 tonnes not recovered. 2,700 out of 6,000 is 45%. The rest may have evaporated, dispersed into the water, sunk or stranded on beaches.
caption: Skimming and sorbents recovered 2,700 of 6,000 tonnes: 45%.
